verses.text: 32. The world: starting from movement, becoming, contingency, and the world’s order and beauty, one can come to a knowledge of God as the origin and the end of the universe. As St. Paul says of the Gentiles: For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. Ever since the creation of the world his invisible nature, namely, his eternal power and deity, has been clearly perceived in the things that have been made. (Rom 1:19–20; cf. Acts 14:15, 17; 17:27–28; Wis 13:1–9.)

216. God’s truth is his wisdom, which commands the whole created order and governs the world. (Cf. Wis 13:1–9.) God, who alone made heaven and earth, can alone impart true knowledge of every created thing in relation to himself. (Cf. Ps 115:15; Wis 7:17–21.)

41. All creatures bear a certain resemblance to God, most especially man, created in the image and likeness of God. The manifold perfections of creatures — their truth, their goodness, their beauty — all reflect the infinite perfection of God. Consequently we can name God by taking his creatures’ perfections as our starting point, “for from the greatness and beauty of created things comes a corresponding perception of their Creator.” (Wis 13:5.)
